newsitem.title: HONG KONG: A new life in London suburbs - by HK governor wife.
newsitem.headline: A new life in London suburbs - by HK governor wife.

text.p: The wife of Hong Kong's governor says they plan a new life in a London suburb near the River Thames -- a far cry from their imposing mansion in Britain's last colonial outpost.
Lavender Patten and her husband Chris, the first career politician chosen as governor, leave Hong Kong after midnight on June 30 when Britain hands the territory back to China after 156 years.

Walking through the grandeur of Government House as workmen packed away their possessions, Mary Lavender St Leger Patten talked in an interview with Hong Kong's Sunday Morning Post of the couple's five-year stint here and their future.
They plan a break at their summer retreat in France and she is negotiating to buy an ordinary suburban house between the southwest London suburbs of Putney and Barnes.
This is an up-market area of the British capital but still a long way from Government House, its guards, servants, tennis court, swimming pool, gardens and the life of a popular, powerful governor.

The sale is expected to be completed in September while the couple unwind in France and Mrs Patten is convinced that life in a Putney house -- with resident dogs and visiting daughters -- will be "very normal", according to the Post.
The "first dogs" Whisky and Soda, which spent a lot of their time whizzing round the ankles of distinguished visitors at diplomatic receptions, fly to France on Sunday night.

"There is quite a bit of common (public land) for the dogs, not far from the river," she said. "I'll probably go over to England a fair amount...I'll be looking after it and getting a few things done for it."
Their French home, bought a couple of years ago and furnished with Chinese elmwood and lacquerwork, is a cottage in "the middle of nowhere", an hour's drive from the southern city of Toulouse.

"We'll miss a lot of friends...the excitement, that buzz and bustle Hong Kong has," she told interviewer Ruth Mathewson. "I'm not sure anywhere else has it in quite the same way. Perhaps in New York you get a bit of it.

"I think you only have to look around Hong Kong and see how well it's doing, the confidence in the economy and the confidence among most people. I really do think that shows that it all actually worked, the five years we've been here.

"I hope that it will continue. Hong Kong people were promised a steady progress to democracy in the (Sino-British) Joint Declaration and the Basic Law. After living in a period in which democracy has increased, I'm sure they will insist on those promises being upheld."

Patten, a former Conservative Party chairman in Britain, was reviled by China after he introduced mild democratic reforms here. "There certainly were times when it was quite difficult," said Lavender Patten, saying her job had been to give support in the background and "a bit of tender, loving care when he needed it".
